title: Your Video Did Not Lose People in the Edit. It Lost Them Before the First Sentence Ended.
markdown:
# Your Video Did Not Lose People in the Edit. It Lost Them Before the First Sentence Ended.

At 0:01, the creator says, "Hey guys, welcome back to the channel." The clip is clean. The lighting is fine. The topic is useful. A thumb flicks upward anyway.

![Three Hook Lab hooks for one video](https://uploads.postiz.com/WHUEBItFNl.png)

That small exit is easy to blame on an algorithm, a crowded feed, or a bad posting time. Usually the simpler answer hurts more: the opening made the viewer wait for the reason to care. On a short-form feed, waiting is the one thing people do not have to do.

The first three seconds do not need a slogan. They need a change in the viewer's attention. A good hook makes someone think, "That is my problem," or "I want to see where this goes." A weak one announces the video before it earns the right to be watched.

## Start with the moment that makes the video necessary

Most intros begin with the creator's plan: who they are, what the video will cover, why they made it. Viewers arrive with a different question: why should I give this the next ten seconds?

Put the friction first. If the video is about a meal-prep method, do not open with "Today I am sharing three meal-prep tips." Open with the container of sad leftovers and the line that names the failure: "I kept spending Sunday cooking lunches I did not want by Tuesday." The subject can wait. The problem cannot.

This also keeps the hook honest. You do not need to promise a life-changing result. You need to make a specific promise the clip can keep. "I tried the five-minute version for a week" gives the viewer a clear question. They stay to find out whether it worked.

## Give the opening one job

A hook often collapses because it tries to carry the entire video. It names the topic, adds context, proves expertise, asks for a follow, and squeezes in a joke. By the time the actual point arrives, the viewer has gone.

Write the opening as a handoff. First, name the tension. Then show the evidence, the attempt, or the answer. If the video is a tutorial, show the ugly before-state before explaining the steps. If it is a review, say what surprised you before listing features. If it is a story, begin at the decision that made the story worth telling.

Read the first line without the rest of the script. Does it create a question that the next shot answers? If it only describes the category of video, it is still an introduction.

## Make five openings before choosing one

The first hook that comes to mind is often the safest version. Safe is a problem in a feed where every clip asks for the same scarce thing: another second.

Try five approaches to the same idea. One can start with the failed result. Another can begin with an unpopular opinion you can defend. A third can show a visual contradiction. One might simply state the specific outcome the viewer wants. The goal is not to manufacture drama. It is to find the clearest entrance to the real video.

Then say each version aloud. The best written hook can still sound like a title read into a microphone. Keep the version that sounds like something a person would say while showing a friend the thing that caught them off guard.

## Cut the throat-clearing

Creators often know their material so well that they warm up on camera. The first take includes the greeting, the setup, the qualifier, and the sentence that finally gets interesting. Cut until that sentence becomes the first one.

This can feel abrupt when you are editing. That is fine. The feed is abrupt already. Your job is not to reproduce the polite beginning of a conversation. It is to make the viewer feel that arriving here was a good decision.

Hook Lab is useful when you have the topic but keep landing on openings that explain too much or sound like everybody else's. Give it the premise and the audience, compare a few angles, and keep the one that makes the next line inevitable: https://capafy.ai/agent/8123079349?ct=hooklab_blog

Before you post, watch the opening once with the sound off and once with it on. With sound off, can the first image carry some tension? With sound on, does the first sentence earn the next? If either answer is no, rewrite those three seconds. They are doing more work than the rest of the clip.
